newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan pleased by Israeli halt of Jerusalem plan.
newsitem.headline: Jordan pleased by Israeli halt of Jerusalem plan.

text.p: Jordan said on Tuesday it was optimistic Israel's move to halt plans to build a new Jewish settler enclave in Arab East Jerusalem would restart stalled peace talks.

Foreign Minister Fayez al-Tarawnah said at the end of a meeting between Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy and King Hussein that Jordan was optimistic Israeli-Palestinian talks would move forward after Israel defused tension by putting brakes on the new settler plan.

Israel's Interior Ministry suspended a permit granted to a U.S. Jewish land baron to build 70 Jewish homes in Ras al-Amoud Arab neighbourhood until an appeal by two left-wing Jerusalem city council members against the plan had been heard.
"Our main concern is lack of progress on the Israeli-Palestinian track and we are encouraged by the recent developments," Tarawnah told reporters at Raghdan Palace, flanked by Levy.

Levy said he briefed King Hussein on his meeting with PLO negotiator Nabil Shaath on Monday, saying the decision by the two sides to renew talks on outstanding issues from a 1995 peace deal was an "important step which will give a boost to peace."

Tarawnah earlier told reporters that Jordan considered Israel's move to suspend the Ras al-Amoud plan a major confidence building step to rebuild trust and "definitely put the Palestinian-Israeli talks on the right course."
"Any issue which leads to building confidence will produce good results," he added.
Israeli-PLO peace talks have been in crisis since March when Israel broke ground on the 6,500-home Har Homa settlement on an East Jerusalem hill known to Palestinians as Jabal Abu Ghneim.
Palestinians demand a halt to settlement activity as a condition to restart peace talks.
But Tarawnah stressed talks should also tackle Palestinian prisoner releases and speeding up delayed Israeli troop redeployment from the West Bank to ensure final status talks succeed.
He said it was not enough just to focus on the three issues of Gaza port, its airport and a safe passage between Gaza and the West Bank, which Palestinians say Israel is obstructing progress on.

"I think issues like prisoners, redeployment and security which are main concerns of Israelis and Palestinians should be concentrated on because those would lead the two parties on solid ground when they face the more hot issue of final status," Tarawnah said.
Final status talks on the shape of a permanent settlement have been delayed because outstanding issues in the interim phase of Israeli-Palestinian accords have yet to be resolved.
Tarawnah also said Jordan was assured by Levy that Netanyahu was against the Ras al-Amoud plan, but warned that if it did go ahead it would create a setback in peace talks.

"We got assurances that the Israeli government is strongly against this decision and God willing we shall not see it (implemented) because we believe it will be another hurdle in the direction of progress in peace," Tarawnah told Reuters.

Israel, which annexed East Jerusalem after capturing it in 1967, says it can build where it likes in the city it calls its united capital. Palestinians say East Jerusalem will be the capital of their future state.
